title: Threads, ownership and deterministic reductions
outcome: Run independent chunks on the prepared two-thread runtime, combine results deterministically and protect shared state with an explicit lock.
key_terms: A macro that schedules a task on any available thread and returns a task whose result `fetch` retrieves.
Unsynchronized access to shared memory by concurrent tasks, at least one of them writing, which can lose updates.
A lock that serializes access to shared state, released in a `finally` block or by the `lock` do-block form.
A task can resume on a different thread after yielding, so scratch storage indexed by `threadid()` is unsafe.
Combining partial results from several tasks, where floating-point regrouping can change the last digits of a sum.
approach: `chunk_squares` splits the input into two index ranges, spawns one task per range that sums squares with `init = 0`, then fetches and adds the two partial sums in a fixed order. `locked_counter` spawns workers that each increment a shared `Ref` inside `lock(guard)`, so every read and write of the counter is protected.

exercises.title: Derive the reduction oracle
exercises.task: Compute the sum of squares through 100 from the closed-form formula.
exercises.answer: The independent formula checks the reduction without copying its loop.
exercises.why: The formula n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 with n = 100 gives 100 times 101 times 201 divided by 6, which is 338350.
exercises.wrong: Checking the threaded result against a serial loop written by the same author shares any indexing mistake with the parallel code.
exercises.verify: Example A asserts `chunk_squares(collect(1:100)) == 338350` five times in a row.

exercises.title: Trace an empty chunk
exercises.task: Explain how the single-element input handles its second range.
exercises.answer: The additive identity makes the empty partial result well-defined.
exercises.why: For `[3]`, `middle = cld(1, 2) = 1`, so the second range is `2:1`, which is empty, and `sum` with `init = 0` returns 0.
exercises.wrong: Dropping `init = 0` makes `sum` over an empty view throw, so a one-element input fails.
exercises.verify: Example A asserts `chunk_squares([3]) == 9`, and the reference checks `chunk_squares([-2, 3]) == 13`.

exercises.title: Explain lost updates
exercises.task: Trace two unprotected increments that read the same value.
exercises.expected: One update can overwrite the other.
exercises.hint: An increment is not one abstract atomic step.
exercises.answer: Locking the full read-modify-write operation prevents this schedule under the stated protocol.
exercises.why: Two tasks can both read 5, both compute 6 and both write 6, so one increment is lost without a lock.
exercises.wrong: Assuming `counter[] += 1` is a single indivisible step predicts the full count even without the lock.
exercises.verify: Example B asserts `locked_counter(4, 100) == 400`; an unprotected owned copy may sometimes print less.

exercises.title: Review scratch ownership
exercises.task: Explain why threadid-indexed buffers can be unsafe.
exercises.hint: A thread ID is not permanent task ownership.
exercises.answer: Task-owned state or explicit synchronization is safer than undocumented schedule assumptions.
exercises.why: Tasks can move between threads, so a buffer indexed by `Threads.threadid()` may be shared by two tasks that both start on one thread.
exercises.wrong: Allocating per-thread buffers by `threadid()` assumes a task keeps its thread for life, which the scheduler does not promise.
exercises.verify: Give each spawned task its own local buffer and confirm results do not depend on the thread count.

exercises.title: Analyze floating reduction
exercises.task: Explain why changing grouping can change floating results.
exercises.hint: Associativity holds for real arithmetic, not all machine arithmetic.
exercises.answer: Use a justified tolerance or a numerically stable reduction when extending the integer example.
exercises.why: Floating addition rounds each partial result, so grouping the sum into two chunks can change the last bits compared with a serial sum.
exercises.wrong: Asserting exact equality between a threaded float reduction and a serial one fails or passes by luck depending on the data.
exercises.verify: Compare float sums with `isapprox` and a stated tolerance; the integer example can stay exact.

exercises.title: Design a performance comparison
exercises.task: State the boundaries needed to claim a parallel speedup.
exercises.expected: Include scheduling, work, reduction and thread configuration.
exercises.answer: Measure the full warmed operation with identical correct outputs and representative data.
exercises.why: A speedup claim must compare warmed runs of the whole operation, with identical correct outputs, on the same thread configuration.
exercises.wrong: Timing 100 small integers once on two threads and calling it faster ignores the scheduling cost that dominates tiny workloads.
exercises.verify: Report the thread count from `Threads.nthreads()`, input size and repeated timings for one and two threads.

checks_note: `[0, 0]` gives 0 through the zero contributions, while `locked_counter(1, 7) == 7` is the serial baseline with no contention. The `before` copy confirms that splitting work into views reads the input without changing it, and the sum of squares of 1, 2 and 3 is 14.
